CNS · Motor System

Physiology of the Basal Ganglia

A subcortical motor control system working alongside the motor cortex and cerebellum to give movement power and precision. This lecture covers the anatomy, circuitry, neurotransmitters, functions, and clinical syndromes of the basal ganglia.

Learning Objectives

  • Name the anatomical and functionally-related components of the basal ganglia and their collective terms (striatum, lentiform nucleus).
  • Trace the cortico-striato-pallido-thalamo-cortical connection.
  • Differentiate the direct excitatory and indirect inhibitory circuits, including neurotransmitters at every step.
  • Explain the role of the substantia nigra, dopamine, and D1/D2 receptors.
  • Describe the caudate circuit vs. putamen circuit and their distinct functional roles.
  • List the functions of the basal ganglia and their effect on muscle tone.
  • Recognize the clinical features of chorea and Parkinson disease and relate each sign back to circuit physiology.

📖 Key Definitions

TermDefinition
Nucleus vs GanglionA collection of neuron cell bodies is called a nucleus if inside the CNS, and a ganglion if outside the CNS (e.g. autonomic ganglia). The basal ganglia are technically nuclei (should correctly be called "basal nuclei") but the historically incorrect name "basal ganglia" persists in common use.
StriatumCollective term for caudate nucleus + putamen. Also called corpus striatum or neostriatum.
Lentiform (lenticular) nucleusCollective term for putamen + globus pallidus — named for its lens-like shape.
High-Yield: Basal ganglia + cerebellum both cooperate with the motor cortex to give movement power (basal ganglia) and help achieve the intended target with precision (cerebellum). All three centers work together for coordinated, accurate movement.
Neuroanatomy

Nuclei & Terminology

The basal ganglia comprise three anatomical nuclei and two functionally-related nuclei.

✅ Anatomically + Physiologically part of BG

  • Caudate nucleus (nucleus caudata)
  • Putamen
  • Globus pallidus

🔗 Functionally related only (not anatomically part of BG)

  • Subthalamic nucleus
  • Substantia nigra — "nigra" = black/dark, referring to its dark pigmented color

🧩 Collective Terminology (High-Yield)

Collective NameStructures CombinedNotes
StriatumCaudate nucleus + PutamenAlso called corpus striatum or neostriatum. Main receiving/input structure of the basal ganglia.
Lentiform (Lenticular) nucleusPutamen + Globus pallidusNamed for its lens (lentiform = lens-shaped) appearance on cross-section.
🧠 Memory trick: Caudate + Putamen = Striatum ("CP = Stripes"). Putamen + Globus pallidus = Lentiform ("PG = lens-shaped"). The Putamen is the shared member of both groups — the anatomical "bridge."

Neurophysiology

🔗 The Cortico-Basal Ganglia Loop

The basal ganglia connect to the cerebral cortex, the substantia nigra, and the brainstem.

1️⃣ Connection with the Cerebral Cortex

From the motor area of the cerebral cortex (mainly area 6) → striatum → globus pallidus → thalamus (ventroanterior & ventrolateral nuclei — the two relay motor nuclei) → back to the motor area of the cortex (area 4).

This is called the Cortico-Striato-Pallido-Thalamo-Cortical Connection

High-Yield: The globus pallidus is almost always the exit point — the majority of outgoing fibers leaving the basal ganglia depart via the globus pallidus toward the thalamus.

🌀 Two Functional Circuits

Direct Excitatory Circuit

Regulates voluntary movements. If it dominates → hyperkinesia (excess movement).

Indirect Inhibitory Circuit

Prevents unwanted involuntary movements. If it dominates → hypokinesia (reduced movement).

Clinical logic: Voluntary movement continues smoothly via the direct circuit, while unwanted involuntary movement is actively suppressed via the indirect circuit. Disease disrupting this balance — e.g. chorea — lets involuntary movements overwhelm voluntary ones.

2️⃣ Connection with the Substantia Nigra

Substantia nigra neurons send axons that terminate on neurons in the striatum, secreting dopamine (the nigrostriatal fiber). Dopamine has two opposite receptor effects:

  • Stimulates D1 receptors → stimulates the GABAergic neurons of the direct circuit.
  • Stimulates D2 receptors → inhibits the GABAergic neurons of the indirect circuit.

3️⃣ Connection with the Brainstem

As the basal ganglia are part of the extrapyramidal system.

⚡ Direct & Indirect Circuits

Trace each neurotransmitter step-by-step. Toggle between circuits on the interactive diagram below.

Glutamate (excitatory) GABA (inhibitory) Dopamine / Acetylcholine Cortex Thalamus
Click any box on the diagram for a quick explanation. Use the tabs above to isolate the direct or indirect pathway.
Reference diagram — Direct vs Indirect Pathway🔍 Click to zoom
This is the canonical circuit diagram matching the interactive version above — use it to double check every neurotransmitter sign (+/–) at each synapse.

🟢 Direct Circuit — Step by Step

  1. Motor cortex → releases glutamate (excitatory) → excites striatum.
  2. Striatum (now excited) → intrastriatal fiber releases acetylcholine (further excites striatum internally).
  3. Excited striatum → sends GABA (inhibitory) → inhibits globus pallidus interna (GPi).
  4. GPi is normally tonically inhibitory (GABA) to the thalamus — but GPi is now itself inhibited ("negative × negative = positive").
  5. Result: thalamus is disinhibited → increased thalamic stimulation → thalamus sends glutamate (excitatory) back to cortex.

Net effect: facilitates voluntary movement. If this circuit dominates → hyperkinesia.

🔴 Indirect Circuit — Step by Step

  1. Motor cortex → releases glutamate → excites striatum (via intrastriatal acetylcholine as before).
  2. Excited striatum → sends GABA → inhibits globus pallidus externa (GPe).
  3. GPe is normally tonically inhibitory to the subthalamic nucleus (STN) — but GPe is now itself inhibited, so STN is disinhibited.
  4. STN → releases glutamate (excitatory) → excites GPi, which is itself inhibitory to the thalamus.
  5. Result: GPi's inhibitory output to the thalamus is increased → thalamus is more inhibited → decreased glutamate to cortex.

Net effect: suppresses unwanted movement. If this circuit dominates → hypokinesia.

🧠 The "double negative" rule: In the direct path, inhibition hits an inhibitor once (− × − = +) → net excitation of thalamus. In the indirect path, inhibition hits an inhibitor twice before reaching GPi (− × − × − = −) → net inhibition of thalamus. Same starting signal (cortical glutamate), opposite final effect, purely because of one extra relay (GPe → STN) in the indirect path.
Neurophysiology

⚫ Substantia Nigra & Neurotransmitters

Four key neurotransmitters govern basal ganglia circuitry — know the origin, target, and effect of each.

NeurotransmitterSecreted byEffect
GlutamateOutput neurons of cerebral cortex, subthalamic nucleus & thalamusExcitatory
AcetylcholineIntrastriatal fibers (inside the corpus striatum)Excitatory
GABAOutput neurons of the striatum & globus pallidus (external & internal)Inhibitory
DopamineSubstantia nigra neurons (nigrostriatal fiber)Excitatory via D1 (direct circuit) / Inhibitory via D2 (indirect circuit)

Dopamine's Dual-Receptor Action

D1 Receptors → Direct Circuit

Dopamine stimulates D1 receptors → stimulates the GABAergic neurons of the direct circuit → net effect is facilitation of movement.

D2 Receptors → Indirect Circuit

Dopamine stimulates D2 receptors → inhibits the GABAergic neurons of the indirect circuit → removes suppression, again facilitating movement.

High-Yield takeaway: Whether acting on D1 or D2, dopamine's net overall effect is to facilitate movement — this is exactly why dopamine deficiency (Parkinson disease) produces poverty of movement (bradykinesia/akinesia).
Neurophysiology

🌀 Caudate Circuit vs Putamen Circuit

Both circuits follow the same cortex → striatum → globus pallidus → thalamus → cortex pattern, but through different parts of the striatum, and serve different functional roles.

Caudate Circuit (Fig. 56–12)🔍 Zoom
Prefrontal, premotor/supplemental, and primary motor/somatosensory cortex ↔ Caudate ↔ Globus pallidus ↔ VA/VL thalamus ↔ back to cortex.
Putamen Circuit (Fig. 56–11)🔍 Zoom
Same cortical inputs ↔ Putamen ↔ Globus pallidus ↔ VA/VL thalamus ↔ back to cortex.
CircuitPathwayFunction
Caudate CircuitCortex (mainly prefrontal & association areas) → Caudate → Putamen → Globus pallidus → Thalamus → back to CortexWith cortical association areas: planning & programming the sequence of cognitive complex movements — e.g. deciding how to move while "facing danger" and needing to think through the escape route.
Putamen CircuitCortex → Putamen → Globus pallidus → Thalamus → back to CortexHelps the corticospinal (pyramidal) system execute slow, sustained, learned movements — e.g. writing, walking, and aspects of vocalization. Involves skill and posture-setting.
Clinical correlation: Because speech (vocalization) requires the ordered, sequential activation of one muscle group before another — much like writing or dressing — basal ganglia lesions can impair this sequencing and contribute to a form of aphasia (slow, monotonous speech in Parkinson disease is a related manifestation).
Neurophysiology

🎯 Functions of the Basal Ganglia

1. Initiate & Regulate Gross Spontaneous (Subconscious) Movement

  • Swinging of the arms while walking — an automatic, subconscious movement associated with the voluntary act of walking.
  • Facial expressions — subconscious muscle contractions that occur spontaneously in association with emotions (you don't consciously choose to change your expression when you hear good or bad news — it happens automatically).
Clinical correlation: Parkinson disease patients lose this associated facial movement, producing a non-expressive "mask face."

2. Putamen Circuit — Slow Sustained Movements

Helps the corticospinal (pyramidal) system execute slow, sustained movements such as writing, walking, and some aspects of vocalization — all of which require skill and correct posture-setting.

3. Caudate Circuit — Planning Cognitive Movement

With the cortical association areas, the caudate circuit is responsible for planning and programming the sequence of cognitively-guided complex movements (e.g. reacting appropriately while facing a sudden danger).

4. Globus Pallidus — Setting Posture

Sets the suitable body posture for performance of a particular movement — e.g. assuming the correct posture of the trunk and limbs to enable writing.

Neurophysiology · High Yield

💪 Muscle Tone & Rigidity

All basal ganglia components except the caudate nucleus exert an inhibitory effect on muscle tone, mediated via the medullary reticular formation, which acts on the gamma motor neuron. This inhibition mainly affects the axial and proximal flexor muscle groups (orthostatic posture).

Why lesions cause a flexed posture

The basal ganglia normally inhibit the extensors. When a basal ganglia lesion removes this inhibition, the extensors become hyperactive — but because the net inhibitory tone on axial/flexor muscles is lost, the overall result is a flexed posture with increased flexor tone.

High-Yield: A lesion in the basal ganglia always produces hypertonia in the form of rigidity — never flaccidity.

Two Types of Rigidity

Lead-Pipe Rigidity

Named for a lead pipe: constant, smooth resistance throughout the range of passive movement — resists you, then finally bends, but with no ratchet-like catching.

Cogwheel Rigidity

Named for a cogwheel/gear: a jerky, catch-and-release resistance during passive movement — produced when a resting tremor is superimposed on the underlying lead-pipe rigidity.

Diseases & Disorders

🔬 Chorea

High Yield

Definition

From Latin/Greek choreia = "dance." A syndrome of involuntary, purposeless, dance-like movements that occur at rest and are increased by voluntary muscular activity and emotions. Normal voluntary movement is interrupted and replaced by dancing-type movement of the upper limb, neck, face, and shoulders.

Pathophysiology

Caused mainly by degeneration of the caudate nucleus (putamen may also be involved). This leads to loss of the inhibitory GABA effect normally exerted on the globus pallidus and substantia nigra → loss of inhibition on the motor cortex → choreic (involuntary dance-like) movements appear.

Hypotonia also occurs, due to loss of the facilitatory effect of the caudate nucleus on muscle tone (recall: the caudate nucleus is the exception that facilitates rather than inhibits tone) — giving a characteristic pendular knee-jerk.

Key Clinical Type

Huntington's chorea — a hereditary (genetic) disease that typically presents later in life (30s–40s) and is accompanied by dementia.
FeatureChorea
Movement qualityInvoluntary, purposeless, dance-like
Site of lesionCaudate nucleus (± putamen)
Aggravating factorsMuscular activity, emotions
ToneHypotonia (pendular knee-jerk)
Hereditary formHuntington's chorea (with dementia, onset 30s–40s)
Diseases & Disorders

🚨 Parkinson Disease (Paralysis Agitans)

Must Know

Etiology & Risk Factors (Causes)

  • Senility — mainly after age 65 (vascular causes)
  • Repeated head trauma
  • Excessive use of dopamine antagonists (antipsychotic drugs)
  • Use of synthetic heroin containing neurotoxins

Pathophysiology

Results from widespread degeneration of the substantia nigra, which normally secretes dopamine into the striatum. Degeneration → ↓ dopamine → the normal dopamine/acetylcholine balance is lost → acetylcholine becomes dominant (relative excess). Treatment therefore aims to restore this balance: give dopamine (as L-DOPA) and/or give anti-cholinergic drugs.

Clinical Manifestations — Three Principal Features

1. Rigidity

Lead-pipe rigidity of all muscles, but affecting mainly the flexor group (flexion attitude) and proximal limb muscles.

2. Static (Resting) Tremor

Involuntary rhythmic movements occurring mainly at rest, described as "pill-rolling" movements. May disappear with voluntary activity — hence the alternate name paralysis agitans ("agitans" = shaking).

3. Akinesia / Bradykinesia (Paralysis)

Occurs due to rigidity, leading to:

  • Masked face — due to loss of facial expression
  • Loss of associated subconscious movements, e.g. swinging of the arm while walking
  • Slow, monotonous speech
  • Short shuffling gait ("festinating gait")
Parkinson's Disease — full body symptom map🔍 Zoom
Parkinson's Disease — posture & gait profile🔍 Zoom

Hypokinetic vs Hyperkinetic Features — The Classic Mix

Hypokinetic (↓ movement)

  • Bradykinesia
  • Akinesia
  • Mask face

Hyperkinetic (↑ activity)

  • Resting (static) tremor
  • Rigidity
Exam favorite: Parkinson disease is a single disease that produces both hypokinetic and hyperkinetic manifestations at the same time — because the direct circuit is under-active (→ bradykinesia/akinesia) while the loss of dopaminergic control also unmasks tremor and rigidity from imbalanced circuit activity and loss of inhibitory tone.
Why does the tremor disappear with movement? The resting tremor is generated by circuit oscillations active during rest; once voluntary (direct circuit-driven) movement begins, cortical drive overrides the abnormal oscillatory activity.

Why the mask face? Facial expression is a basal-ganglia-mediated subconscious movement; with degeneration, this associated movement is lost.

Why short shuffling (festinating) gait? The patient's flexed, forward-tilted posture shifts the center of gravity forward; short rapid steps occur as the patient appears to "chase" and catch up with their own center of gravity to avoid falling.
High-Yield Exam Zone

⭐ High-Yield Exam & Clinical Pearls

⭐⭐⭐ High-Yield Exam Pearls

  • Basal Ganglia Circuits: the primary connection is the cortico-striato-pallido-thalamo-cortical connection. The direct excitatory circuit facilitates voluntary movement (hyperkinesia if unchecked); the indirect inhibitory circuit suppresses unwanted involuntary movement (hypokinesia if unchecked).
  • Neurotransmitters: Glutamate is the primary excitatory neurotransmitter (Cortex→Striatum; Subthalamic Nucleus→Globus Pallidus; Thalamus→Cortex). GABA is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter (Striatum→Globus Pallidus; Globus Pallidus→Thalamus).
  • Dopamine Receptors: Dopamine from the substantia nigra stimulates D1 receptors (excitatory to the direct pathway) and inhibits D2 receptors (inhibitory to the indirect pathway). Net effect of dopamine is facilitating movement.
  • Parkinson Disease Pathology: caused by degeneration of the substantia nigra, leading to decreased dopamine and an imbalance where acetylcholine dominates.
  • Parkinson Disease Presentation Mix: exhibits both hypokinetic signs (bradykinesia, akinesia, mask face) and hyperkinetic signs (resting tremor, rigidity).
  • Chorea Pathology: caused by degeneration of the caudate nucleus and putamen, removing inhibition on the motor cortex and resulting in involuntary, dance-like movements.
  • Muscle Tone: the basal ganglia (except the caudate nucleus) generally exert an inhibitory effect on muscle tone via the medullary reticular formation. Lesions typically produce hypertonia (rigidity).

🩺 Clinical Pearls

  • Mask Face: facial expressions are subconscious movements regulated by the basal ganglia. Loss of this regulation in Parkinson disease leads to a non-expressive, "mask-like" appearance.
  • Gait and Posture: loss of basal ganglia inhibition on axial extensors forces Parkinson's patients into a characteristic flexion attitude (bent forward). They also lose the subconscious swinging of the arms while walking.
  • Festinating Gait: the characteristic Parkinsonian walk is a short shuffling gait where the patient appears to be hurrying to catch up with their own center of gravity to prevent falling.
  • Resting vs. Action Tremor: the typical Parkinsonian pill-rolling tremor is a static (resting) tremor that occurs when the limb is supported and at rest, notably disappearing or decreasing with voluntary action.
  • Assessing Rigidity: when examining muscle tone in basal ganglia lesions, you will feel lead-pipe rigidity (continuous, smooth resistance) or cogwheel rigidity (a jerky, clicking resistance caused by the superimposition of tremor over the rigidity).
  • Aphasia and Basal Ganglia: the execution of complex sequence movements like writing or speaking requires basal ganglia programming. Lesions can result in expressive difficulties (aphasia) due to improper sequencing of vocal muscle contractions.

Memory & Mnemonics

🧠 Memory Aids

Striatum vs Lentiform: "CP-Stripes, PG-Lens" — Caudate+Putamen = Striatum (stripes); Putamen+Globus pallidus = Lentiform (lens-shaped). Putamen is shared by both.
Direct = "D for Do it": Direct circuit → excites thalamus → facilitates movement (go/do). Indirect = "I for Inhibit it": extra relay through GPe/STN → net inhibition of thalamus → suppresses movement.
Double-negative rule: One inhibition-of-an-inhibitor (direct) = excitation. Two inhibitions-of-inhibitors in series (indirect) = inhibition. Count the negatives!
D1 = "1 Direct": D1 receptor → direct circuit → excitatory. D2 = "2 for the 2nd (indirect), inhibits": D2 receptor → indirect circuit → inhibitory (removing the brake).
Chorea = Caudate: both start with "C" — Chorea comes from Caudate degeneration. Parkinson = Pigment loss: Parkinson comes from Substantia Nigra (pigmented, dopamine) degeneration.
TRAP for Parkinson disease: Tremor (resting/pill-rolling), Rigidity (lead-pipe/cogwheel), Akinesia/bradykinesia, Posture instability (stooped, festinating gait).
Lead-pipe vs Cogwheel: Lead-pipe = smooth continuous resistance (like bending a solid pipe). Cogwheel = lead-pipe rigidity + tremor superimposed = jerky "gear-like" catches.

📚 Full Lecture Transcript

Complete bilingual (Arabic/English) transcript, organized by topic. Nothing omitted from the original recording.

1. Introduction — Association of BG, Cerebellum & Motor Cortex

صوره نظيفه للي بيورينا التقسيمه حقت الـ basal ganglia. طيب حنتكلم عن anatomy of basal ganglia. الـ basal ganglia ومعاها الـ cerebellum ديل مع بعض بيشتغلوا مع الـ motor cortex ليه؟ التعاون بتاعهم مع الـ motor cortex ده عشان الـ power بتاعت الـ movement وعشان الـ movement تكون precise، تكون دقيقة. يعني إنت داير تصل هدف معين، تصل للهدف المعين بالحركة بتاعتك. لكن بتصليهو بعدين أكتر مع منو؟ مع الـ cerebellum. فهم التلاتة بيشتغلوا مع بعض.

The basal ganglia and cerebellum have an association with the motor cortex: to give the power and precision of muscle activity. The three centers work together so movement is both powerful and accurate in reaching a target.

2. Anatomical Components & Terminology (Nucleus vs Ganglion)

الـ basal ganglia بتشمل three large cerebral nuclei. طبعا هي أساسا يفترض يسموها basal nuclei، ده الاسم الحقيقي، ده الاسم الصحيح. ليه؟ لأنه عندنا مصطلحين هنا: مصطلح ganglion ومصطلح nucleus. لمن الـ collection بتاعت الـ neuron bodies تكون في الـ CNS بيسموها nucleus. ولمن تكون outside the CNS بيسموها ganglion.

The basal ganglia include three large cerebral nuclei. They should really be called "basal nuclei" — the correct term — because a collection of neuron bodies inside the CNS is called a nucleus, while outside the CNS it is called a ganglion (e.g. autonomic ganglia). Because the incorrect name became common usage, we still call them "basal ganglia," even though they are truly nuclei: caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus (anatomically and physiologically part of the basal ganglia), plus the subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra (functionally related, but not anatomically part of the basal ganglia). "Nigra" refers to the dark color of the substantia nigra.

3. Striatum & Lentiform Nucleus + Atlas Images

المصطلحات الجاية دي مهمة جدا. الـ caudate ومعاها الـ putamen مع بعض بيسموهم corpus striatum أو بيسموهم neo striatum أو تقول just striatum. المصطلح بتاع lentiform nucleus... دي بتجمع منو؟ ده الـ putamen مع الـ globus pallidus.

Caudate + putamen together are called corpus striatum / neostriatum / striatum. Lentiform (lenticular) nucleus = putamen + globus pallidus, named for its lens-like shape. The speaker then walks through the labeled coronal section slides identifying caudate (blue), putamen, substantia nigra (dark color), and subthalamic nucleus (nucleus subthalamicus, below the thalamus) — both functionally part of the basal ganglia.

4. Cortical Connection — Cortico-Striato-Pallido-Thalamo-Cortical Loop

الـ connection بتاعت الـ basal ganglia. أول connection مع الـ cerebral cortex... من الـ motor area بتاعت الـ cerebral cortex، mainly area 6، بتمشي الـ fiber للـ striatum... من الـ corpus striatum بتمشي الـ fiber للـ globus pallidus ومنه للـ thalamus اللي هو الـ ventroanterior والـ ventrolateral thalamic nuclei.

From the motor area of the cortex (mainly area 6) → striatum → globus pallidus → thalamus (ventroanterior and ventrolateral relay motor nuclei) → back to cortex. This whole loop is called the cortico-striato-pallido-thalamo-cortical connection. The globus pallidus is nearly always the exit point of fibers leaving the basal ganglia. Functionally this loop is divided into two circuits: the direct excitatory circuit (regulates voluntary movement) and the indirect inhibitory circuit (prevents unwanted movement) — disruption of this balance produces disorders like chorea.

5. Direct Circuit — Neurotransmitter Walkthrough

الـ motor cortex بتمشي تعمل تنبيه في الـ striatum عبر منو؟ glutamate... الـ striatum بيكون بيرسل fiber، بتطلع GABA عشان يمشي للـ globus pallidus internal segment... الـ thalamus حيحصل ليه شنو؟ excitation.

Motor cortex excites the striatum via glutamate. The excited striatum sends GABA to inhibit GPi. GPi is itself normally inhibitory (GABA) to the thalamus — so inhibiting GPi disinhibits the thalamus, increasing its stimulation. The thalamus then excites the cortex via glutamate. If this circuit dominates ("becomes too strong"), the result is hyperkinetic movement; in balance, it produces normal voluntary movement.

6. Indirect Circuit — Neurotransmitter Walkthrough

نجي للاتجاه المعاكس. الـ indirect... نفس الـ glutamate اشتغل في الـ striatum طلع acetylcholine، الـ striatum excited. قام الـ striatum مشى بـ GABA... عمل inhibition للـ globus pallidus externa... عشان كده النتيجة حتكون شنو؟ inhibition.

Same starting excitation: cortical glutamate excites the striatum (with intrastriatal acetylcholine). The excited striatum sends GABA to inhibit GPe. GPe is normally inhibitory to the subthalamic nucleus (STN) — inhibiting GPe disinhibits STN, so STN's glutamate output increases, exciting GPi (which is itself inhibitory to the thalamus). Net effect: the thalamus receives more inhibition, and glutamate output to cortex decreases → this circuit is responsible for hypokinetic (suppressive) control, balancing the direct circuit's excitatory drive.

7. Substantia Nigra Connection & Dopamine Receptors

الـ connection التاني مع الـ substantia nigra. الـ neuron بتاعت الـ substantia nigra بترسل الـ axon بتاعتها لـ terminate في neuron في الـ striatum، بتطلع dopamine... الـ dopamine لما يرتبط بـ D1 receptor stimulate الـ GABAergic neuron of the direct circuit. والـ dopamine لما ينبه D2 inhibit الـ GABAergic neuron of the indirect circuit.

Substantia nigra neurons project (nigrostriatal fiber) to terminate on striatal neurons, releasing dopamine. Dopamine binding D1 receptors stimulates the GABAergic neurons of the direct circuit (increases inhibitory tone within that loop, which as shown ultimately facilitates movement); dopamine binding D2 receptors inhibits the GABAergic neurons of the indirect circuit (reduces suppression, also facilitating movement). Also connects with the brainstem as part of the extrapyramidal system — glutamate acts at three locations: cortex→striatum, subthalamic nucleus→thalamus-directed fiber, and thalamus→cortex; all three are excitatory, and the net effect at any moment depends on which pathway is being increased or decreased.

8. Summary of Neurotransmitters

أهو ده الـ glutamate هنا excitatory... الـ acetylcholine ده قلنا intra-striatal fiber... GABA inhibitory بيطلع من الـ output neuron بتاعت الـ striatum... والـ dopamine secreted بالـ substantia nigra.

Glutamate is excitatory at three sites (cortex→striatum, STN→GPi, thalamus→cortex). Acetylcholine is excitatory, released by intrastriatal fibers within the striatum. GABA is inhibitory, released by output neurons of the striatum toward GPi/GPe. Dopamine is secreted by substantia nigra neurons: excitatory via D1, inhibitory via D2 — whichever receptor is stimulated determines whether the downstream GABAergic neuron is turned up or down.

9. Caudate Circuit vs Putamen Circuit

الـ connection دي الـ بيسموها اللي هما عندي two circuits دي الـ caudate circuit والـ putamen circuit... ده سميناه قبيل cortico-striato-pallido-thalamo-cortical connection.

Both circuits begin at the cortex (more from pre-motor/supplementary areas for caudate) and follow the same general cortex→striatum→pallidum→thalamus→cortex route — one passing through the caudate, the other through the putamen — both ultimately called the cortico-striato-pallido-thalamo-cortical connection, just through different striatal input points.

10. Functions of the Basal Ganglia

أول وظيفة للـ basal ganglia، initiate and regulate gross spontaneous movement... زي الـ swinging arms while walking... الحاجة التانية المهمة جدا زي الـ facial expression... عشان كده العيانين بتاعين الـ Parkinson disease بيقول لك عندهم non-expressive face.

The basal ganglia initiate and regulate gross, spontaneous (subconscious) movement: e.g. swinging arms while walking, and facial expressions in association with emotions (automatic, not consciously controlled) — lost in Parkinson disease, producing the "mask face." The putamen circuit helps the corticospinal (pyramidal) system execute slow sustained movements like writing, walking, and vocalization — these all involve skill and posture-setting, and basal ganglia lesions can therefore contribute to aphasia through disordered muscle sequencing. The caudate circuit, with cortical association areas, plans and programs sequences of cognitive movement (e.g. reacting while facing danger). The globus pallidus helps set appropriate posture for skilled movements (e.g. writing).

11. Muscle Tone, Rigidity Types

الـ basal ganglia all except caudate nucleus has inhibitory effect on muscle tone... عشان كده لمن الـ inhibition بتاع الـ basal ganglia يروح، الـ extensor حيحصل ليها شنو؟ حتبقى hyperactive... الـ lesion في الـ basal ganglia always produces hypertonia، اللي هي rigidity... lead-pipe rigidity أو cogwheel rigidity.

All basal ganglia components except the caudate nucleus inhibit muscle tone via the medullary reticular formation acting on gamma motor neurons, mainly affecting axial and proximal flexor muscles. The basal ganglia normally inhibit extensors; when that inhibition is lost, extensors become hyperactive, contributing to a flexed posture. Lesions always produce hypertonia (rigidity) — lead-pipe (smooth, constant resistance, like bending a lead pipe) or cogwheel (jerky, ratchet-like resistance from superimposed tremor).

12. Chorea

نيجي للـ clinical syndromes اللي بتصيب الـ basal ganglia. الأمراض اللي بتصيب الـ basal ganglia، أول واحد عندنا هو الـ Chorea... سببها degeneration في الـ caudate nucleus وفي الـ putamen... ومن أشهر أنواعها Huntington chorea.

Chorea (from Greek/Latin "choreia" = dance) is dance-like involuntary movement caused by degeneration of the caudate nucleus and putamen, which removes the inhibition normally exerted on the motor cortex, allowing involuntary movements to appear. Huntington's chorea is the most famous type — a hereditary disease appearing somewhat later in life (30s–40s) accompanied by dementia.

13. Parkinson Disease — Cause & Treatment Logic

المرض التاني المهم جدا... هو الـ Parkinson disease أو بيسموه paralysis agitans، الشلل الرعاش. ده سببه degeneration في الـ substantia nigra... فلما يحصل degeneration، الـ dopamine حيقل... في العلاج، يا إما ندي dopamine (في شكل L-DOPA)، أو ندي anti-cholinergic drugs.

Parkinson disease (paralysis agitans) is caused by degeneration of the substantia nigra, reducing dopamine output. This shifts the dopamine/acetylcholine balance so acetylcholine dominates. Treatment therefore either replaces dopamine (as L-DOPA) or blocks the relatively excessive cholinergic activity (anticholinergic drugs) to restore balance.

14. Parkinson Disease — Manifestations & Hypo/Hyperkinetic Mix

شنو الـ manifestations بتاعت الـ Parkinson disease؟ أول حاجة، عندنا الـ rigidity... تاني حاجة، الـ tremor... تالت حاجة، الـ bradykinesia أو الـ akinesia... إذن، العيان بتاع الـ Parkinson disease بيجمع بين حاجات hypokinetic وحاجات hyperkinetic.

Manifestations: (1) rigidity — lead-pipe or cogwheel; (2) static/resting tremor — pill-rolling, disappears with voluntary movement; (3) bradykinesia/akinesia — slow to initiate movement, flexed posture, short shuffling ("festinating") gait as the patient hurries to catch up with their own center of gravity, mask face, and loss of arm swing while walking. Parkinson disease therefore combines hypokinetic features (bradykinesia, akinesia, mask face) with hyperkinetic features (tremor, rigidity) — a classic mixed presentation that is heavily tested, along with why the tremor disappears with movement, why the face is masked, and why the gait is short and shuffling — all explained by the physiology and circuits covered above.
